questions.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-5\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{25y}{4}=4{e}^{-x}.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x),$ which is the solution to the homogeneous equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-5\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{25y}{4}=0.
$$

Writing down and solving the auxiliary equation gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-5\lambda +\frac{25}{4} & =0 \\ {(\lambda -\frac{5}{2})}^{2} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So $\lambda =\frac{5}{2}$ is a repeated root, and therefore the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{5x/2}+Bx{e}^{5x/2}.
$$

We now need to find the particular integral ${y}_{p}(x).$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is $4{e}^{-x}.$ In this case, the constant factor in the exponent is $-1$, which is not the root of the auxiliary equation. Therefore, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}=\alpha {e}^{-x},
$$

where $\alpha $ is a constant that is to be determined.

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=-\alpha {e}^{-x},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=\alpha {e}^{-x}.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute ${y}_{p},$ ${y}_{p}^{′},$ and ${y}_{p}^{″}$ into the ODE and solve for $\alpha :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\alpha {e}^{-x}-5(-\alpha {e}^{-x})+\frac{25}{4}\alpha {e}^{-x} & =4{e}^{-x} \\ (1+5+\frac{25}{4})\alpha {e}^{-x} & =4{e}^{-x} \\ \frac{49}{4}\alpha {e}^{-x} & =4{e}^{-x} \\ \frac{49}{4}\alpha  & =4 \\ \alpha  & =\frac{16}{49}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=\frac{16}{49}{e}^{-x}.
$$

The general solution is given by

$$
y(x)={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x),
$$

and therefore, the general solution in our case is

$$
y=A{e}^{5x/2}+Bx{e}^{5x/2}+\frac{16}{49}{e}^{-x}.
$$

questions.problem:
Given that the differential equation 

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+4\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+8y=12{e}^{-2x}
$$

has the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)={e}^{-2x}(P\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡2x),$ find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ to this equation.
questions.worked_solution:
Since the complementary function is ${y}_{c}(x)={e}^{-2x}(P\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡2x),$ the roots of the auxiliary equation are $\lambda =-2\pm 2\text{i}.$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is $12{e}^{-2x}.$ In this case, the constant factor in the exponent is $-2$, which is not the root of the auxiliary equation. Therefore, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}=\alpha {e}^{-2x},
$$

where $\alpha $ is a constant that is to be determined.

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=-2\alpha {e}^{-2x},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=4\alpha {e}^{-2x}\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute ${y}_{p},$ ${y}_{p}^{′},$ and ${y}_{p}^{″}$ into the ODE and solve for $\alpha :$

$$
\begin{aligned}4\alpha {e}^{-2x}+4(-2\alpha {e}^{-2x})+8(\alpha {e}^{-2x}) & =12{e}^{-2x} \\ (4-8+8)\alpha {e}^{-2x} & =12{e}^{-2x} \\ 4\alpha {e}^{-2x} & =12{e}^{-2x} \\ \alpha  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=3{e}^{-2x}.
$$

questions.problem:
Given that the differential equation 

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-9\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+18y=8{e}^{2x}
$$

has the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{3x}+B{e}^{6x}$, find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ to this equation.
questions.worked_solution:
Since the complementary function is ${y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{3x}+B{e}^{6x},$ the roots of the auxiliary equation are $\lambda =3$ and $\lambda =6.$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is $8{e}^{2x}.$ In this case, the constant factor in the exponent is $2$, which is not the root of the auxiliary equation. Therefore, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}=\alpha {e}^{2x},
$$

where $\alpha $ is a constant that is to be determined.

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=2\alpha {e}^{2x},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=4\alpha {e}^{2x}.
$$

We substitute ${y}_{p},$ ${y}_{p}^{′},$ and ${y}_{p}^{″}$ into the ODE and solve for $\alpha :$

$$
\begin{aligned}4\alpha {e}^{2x}-9(2\alpha {e}^{2x})+18(\alpha {e}^{2x}) & =8{e}^{2x} \\ (4-18+18)\alpha {e}^{2x} & =8{e}^{2x} \\ 4\alpha {e}^{2x} & =8{e}^{2x} \\ \alpha  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=2{e}^{2x}.
$$

questions.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-4\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+5y=20{e}^{4x}.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x),$ which is the solution to the homogeneous equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-4\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+5y=0.
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
{\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +5=0.
$$

The auxiliary equation can be solved by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +5 & =0 \\ ({\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +4)-4+5 & =0 \\ (\lambda -2)^{2} & =-1 \\ \lambda -2 & =\pm \text{i} \\ \lambda  & =2\pm \text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{c}(x) & ={e}^{2x}(P\operatorname{cos}⁡x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡x).\end{aligned}
$$

We now need to find the particular integral ${y}_{p}(x).$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is $20{e}^{4x}.$ In this case, the constant factor in the exponent is $4$, which is not the root of the auxiliary equation. Therefore, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}=\alpha {e}^{4x},
$$

where $\alpha $ is a constant that is to be determined.

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=4\alpha {e}^{4x},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=16\alpha {e}^{4x}\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute ${y}_{p},$ ${y}_{p}^{′},$ and ${y}_{p}^{″}$ into the ODE and solve for $\alpha :$

$$
\begin{aligned}16\alpha {e}^{4x}-4(4\alpha {e}^{4x})+5(\alpha {e}^{4x}) & =20{e}^{4x} \\ (16-16+5)\alpha {e}^{4x} & =20{e}^{4x} \\ 5\alpha {e}^{4x} & =20{e}^{4x} \\ 5\alpha  & =20 \\ \alpha  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=4{e}^{4x}.
$$

The general solution is given by

$$
y(x)={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x),
$$

and therefore, the general solution in our case is

$$
y={e}^{2x}(P\operatorname{cos}⁡x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡x)+4{e}^{4x}.
$$

Given that the differential equation 

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+3\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-4y={e}^{-3x}
$$

has the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{x}+B{e}^{-4x}$, find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ to this equation.
questions.worked_solution:
Since the complementary function is ${y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{x}+B{e}^{-4x},$ the roots of the auxiliary equation are $\lambda =1$ and $\lambda =-4.$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is ${e}^{-3x}.$ In this case, the constant factor in the exponent is $-3$, which is not the root of the auxiliary equation. Therefore, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}=\alpha {e}^{-3x},
$$

where $\alpha $ is a constant that is to be determined.

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives:

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=-3\alpha {e}^{-3x},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=9\alpha {e}^{-3x}
$$

We substitute ${y}_{p},$ ${y}_{p}^{′},$ and ${y}_{p}^{″}$ into the ODE and solve for $\alpha :$

$$
\begin{aligned}9\alpha {e}^{-3x}+3(-3\alpha {e}^{-3x})-4(\alpha {e}^{-3x}) & ={e}^{-3x} \\ (9-9-4)\alpha {e}^{-3x} & ={e}^{-3x} \\ -4\alpha {e}^{-3x} & ={e}^{-3x} \\ \alpha  & =-\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=-\frac{1}{4}{e}^{-3x}.
$$

Given that the differential equation 

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-3\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-4y=10{e}^{-x}
$$

has the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{-x}+B{e}^{4x}$, find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ to this equation.
questions.worked_solution:
Since the complementary function is ${y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{-x}+B{e}^{4x},$ the roots of the auxiliary equation are $\lambda =-1$ and $\lambda =4.$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is $10{e}^{-x}.$ In this case, the constant factor in the exponent is $-1$, which coincides with one of the roots of the auxiliary equation. Therefore, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}=\alpha x{e}^{-x}.
$$

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=\alpha (1-x){e}^{-x},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=\alpha (x-2){e}^{-x}.
$$

We substitute ${y}_{p},$ ${y}_{p}^{′},$ and ${y}_{p}^{″}$ into the ODE and solve for $\alpha :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\alpha (x-2){e}^{-x}-3(\alpha (1-x){e}^{-x})-4(\alpha x{e}^{-x}) & =10{e}^{-x} \\ (x-2-3+3x-4x)\alpha {e}^{-x} & =10{e}^{-x} \\ -5\alpha {e}^{-x} & =10{e}^{-x} \\ -5\alpha  & =10 \\ \alpha  & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=-2x{e}^{-x}.
$$

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+3\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2y=4{e}^{-x}.
$$

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+3\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2y=0.
$$

Writing down and solving the auxiliary equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+3\lambda +2 & =0 \\ (\lambda +2)(\lambda +1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So $\lambda =-2$ or $\lambda =-1$, and therefore the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{-2x}+B{e}^{-x}.
$$

We now need to find the particular integral ${y}_{p}(x).$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is $4{e}^{-x}.$ In this case, the constant factor in the exponent is $-1$, which coincides with one of the roots of the auxiliary equation. Therefore, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}=\alpha x{e}^{-x},
$$

where $\alpha $ is a constant that is to be determined.

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=\alpha (1-x){e}^{-x},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=\alpha (x-2){e}^{-x}.
$$

We substitute ${y}_{p},$ ${y}_{p}^{′},$ and ${y}_{p}^{″}$ into the ODE and solve for $\alpha :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\alpha (x-2){e}^{-x}+3(\alpha (1-x){e}^{-x})+2(\alpha x{e}^{-x}) & =4{e}^{-x} \\ (x-2+3-3x+2x)\alpha {e}^{-x} & =4{e}^{-x} \\ \alpha {e}^{-x} & =4{e}^{-x} \\ \alpha  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=4x{e}^{-x}.
$$

$$
y(x)={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x),
$$

$$
y=A{e}^{-2x}+B{e}^{-x}+4x{e}^{-x}.

$$

$$

$$

$$

So $\lambda =-1$ or $\lambda =3$, and therefore the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{-x}+B{e}^{3x}.
$$

We now need to find the particular integral ${y}_{p}(x).$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is $4{e}^{3x}.$ In this case, the constant factor in the exponent is $3$, which coincides with one of the roots of the auxiliary equation. Therefore, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}=\alpha x{e}^{3x},
$$

where $\alpha $ is a constant that is to be determined.

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=\alpha (1+3x){e}^{3x},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=\alpha (9x+6){e}^{3x}.

$$

{y}_{p}(x)=x{e}^{3x}.

$$
y(x)={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x),

$$

$$
{y}_{p}=\alpha x{e}^{-4x}.

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=\alpha (1-4x){e}^{-4x},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=\alpha (16x-8){e}^{-4x}.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\alpha (16x-8){e}^{-4x}+6(\alpha (1-4x){e}^{-4x})+8(\alpha x{e}^{-4x}) & =2{e}^{-4x} \\ (16x-8+6-24x+8x)\alpha {e}^{-4x} & =2{e}^{-4x} \\ -2\alpha {e}^{-4x} & =2{e}^{-4x} \\ -2\alpha  & =2 \\ \alpha  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=-x{e}^{-4x}.

Since the complementary function is ${y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{2x}+Bx{e}^{2x},$ we have that $\lambda =2$ is the double root of the auxiliary equation.

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is $3{e}^{2x}.$  In this case, the constant factor in the exponent is $2$, which coincides with the double root of the auxiliary equation. Therefore, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}=\alpha {x}^{2}{e}^{2x},
$$

where $\alpha $ is a constant that is to be determined.

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=\alpha (2{x}^{2}+2x){e}^{2x},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=\alpha (4{x}^{2}+8x+2){e}^{2x}.

$$
\begin{aligned}\alpha (4{x}^{2}+8x+2){e}^{2x}-4(\alpha (2{x}^{2}+2x){e}^{2x})+4(\alpha {x}^{2}{e}^{2x}) & =3{e}^{2x} \\ (4{x}^{2}+8x+2-8{x}^{2}-8x+4{x}^{2})\alpha {e}^{2x} & =3{e}^{2x} \\ 2\alpha {e}^{2x} & =3{e}^{2x} \\ 2\alpha  & =3 \\ \alpha  & =\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=\frac{3}{2}{x}^{2}{e}^{2x}.

\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-3\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{9}{4}y=0.
$$

Writing down and solving the auxiliary equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-3\lambda +\frac{9}{4} & =0 \\ {(\lambda -\frac{3}{2})}^{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So $\lambda =\frac{3}{2}$ is a repeated root, and therefore the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{3x/2}+Bx{e}^{3x/2}.
$$

We now need to find the particular integral ${y}_{p}(x).$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is $6{e}^{3x/2}.$ In this case, the constant factor in the exponent is $\frac{3}{2}$, which coincides with the double root of the auxiliary equation. Therefore, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}=\alpha {x}^{2}{e}^{3x/2},
$$

where $\alpha $ is a constant that is to be determined.

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=\alpha (2x+\frac{3}{2}{x}^{2}){e}^{3x/2},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=\alpha (2+6x+\frac{9}{4}{x}^{2}){e}^{3x/2}.
$$

We substitute ${y}_{p},$ ${y}_{p}^{′},$ and ${y}_{p}^{″}$ into the ODE and solve for $\alpha :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\alpha (2+6x+\frac{9}{4}{x}^{2}){e}^{3x/2}-3(\alpha (2x+\frac{3}{2}{x}^{2}){e}^{3x/2})+\frac{9}{4}(\alpha {x}^{2}{e}^{3x/2}) & =6{e}^{3x/2} \\ (2+6x+\frac{9}{4}{x}^{2}-6x-\frac{9}{2}{x}^{2}+\frac{9}{4}{x}^{2})\alpha {e}^{3x/2} & =6{e}^{3x/2} \\ 2\alpha {e}^{3x/2} & =6{e}^{3x/2} \\ 2\alpha  & =6 \\ \alpha  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=3{x}^{2}{e}^{3x/2}.
$$

The general solution is given by

$$
y(x)={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x),
$$

and therefore, the general solution in our case is

$$
y=A{e}^{3x/2}+Bx{e}^{3x/2}+3{x}^{2}{e}^{3x/2}.
$$

questions.problem:
Given that the differential equation 

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+6\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+9y=6{e}^{-3x}
$$

has the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{-3x}+Bx{e}^{-3x}$, find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ to this equation.
questions.worked_solution:
Since the complementary function is ${y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{-3x}+Bx{e}^{-3x},$ we have that $\lambda =-3$ is the double root of the auxiliary equation.

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is $6{e}^{-3x}.$  In this case, the constant factor in the exponent is $-3$, which coincides with the double root of the auxiliary equation. Therefore, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}=\alpha {x}^{2}{e}^{-3x},
$$

where $\alpha $ is a constant that is to be determined.

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=\alpha (2x-3{x}^{2}){e}^{-3x},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=\alpha (9{x}^{2}-12x+2){e}^{-3x}.
$$

We substitute ${y}_{p},$ ${y}_{p}^{′},$ and ${y}_{p}^{″}$ into the ODE and solve for $\alpha :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\alpha (9{x}^{2}-12x+2){e}^{-3x}+6(\alpha (2x-3{x}^{2}){e}^{-3x})+9(\alpha {x}^{2}{e}^{-3x}) & =6{e}^{-3x} \\ (9{x}^{2}-12x+2+12x-18{x}^{2}+9{x}^{2})\alpha {e}^{-3x} & =6{e}^{-3x} \\ 2\alpha {e}^{-3x} & =6{e}^{-3x} \\ 2\alpha  & =6 \\ \alpha  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=3{x}^{2}{e}^{-3x}.
$$

questions.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+4\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+4y=4{e}^{-2x}.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x),$ which is the solution to the homogeneous equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+4\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+4y=0.
$$

Writing down and solving the auxiliary equation gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+4\lambda +4 & =0 \\ (\lambda +2)^{2} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So $\lambda =-2$ is a repeated root, and therefore the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{-2x}+Bx{e}^{-2x}.
$$

We now need to find the particular integral ${y}_{p}(x).$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is $4{e}^{-2x}.$ In this case, the constant factor in the exponent is $-2$, which coincides with the double root of the auxiliary equation. Therefore, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}=\alpha {x}^{2}{e}^{-2x},
$$

where $\alpha $ is a constant that is to be determined.

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x} & =\alpha (2x-2{x}^{2}){e}^{-2x},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=\alpha (4{x}^{2}-8x+2){e}^{-2x}.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute ${y}_{p},$ ${y}_{p}^{′},$ and ${y}_{p}^{″}$ into the ODE and solve for $\alpha :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\alpha (4{x}^{2}-8x+2){e}^{-2x}+4\alpha (2x-2{x}^{2}){e}^{-2x}+4\alpha {x}^{2}{e}^{-2x} & =4{e}^{-2x} \\ \alpha (4{x}^{2}-8x+2+8x-8{x}^{2}+4{x}^{2}){e}^{-2x} & =4{e}^{-2x} \\ 2\alpha {e}^{-2x} & =4{e}^{-2x} \\ 2\alpha  & =4 \\ \alpha  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=2{x}^{2}{e}^{-2x}.
$$

The general solution is given by

$$
y(x)={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x),
$$

and therefore, the general solution in our case is

$$
y=A{e}^{-2x}+Bx{e}^{-2x}+2{x}^{2}{e}^{-2x}.
$$

questions.problem:
Given that the differential equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+2\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-3y=8{e}^{x}
$$

has the general solution

$$
y(x)=A{e}^{-3x}+B{e}^{x}+2x{e}^{x},
$$

solve the initial value problem

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+2\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-3y=8{e}^{x},\,y(0)=4,\,{y}^{′}(0)=2.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
We find the constants $A$ and $B$ by substituting the initial conditions.

- Substituting $y(0)=4$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & =A{e}^{-3(0)}+B{e}^{0}+2(0){e}^{0} \\ 4 & =A+B.\end{aligned}
$$

- Differentiating $y$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=-3A{e}^{-3x}+B{e}^{x}+2x{e}^{x}+2{e}^{x}.
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(0)=2$ into the derivative gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =-3A{e}^{-3(0)}+B{e}^{0}+2(0){e}^{0}+2{e}^{0} \\ 2 & =-3A+B+2 \\ 0 & =-3A+B \\ B & =3A.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following system of equations for $A$ and $B:$

$$
{\begin{aligned}A+B=4 \\ B=3A\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $A=1,B=3.$

Finally, since $A=1$ and $B=3,$ we have the following solution to the initial value problem:

$$
y={e}^{-3x}+3{e}^{x}+2x{e}^{x}
$$

questions.problem:
Given that the differential equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-2\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+y=-2{e}^{2x}
$$

has the general solution

$$
y(x)=A{e}^{x}+Bx{e}^{x}-2{e}^{2x},
$$

solve the initial value problem

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-2\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+y=-2{e}^{2x},\,y(0)=0,\,{y}^{′}(0)=0.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
We find the constants $A$ and $B$ by substituting the initial conditions.

- Substituting $y(0)=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =A{e}^{0}+B(0){e}^{0}-2{e}^{2(0)} \\ 0 & =A-2 \\ A & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

- Differentiating $y$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=A{e}^{x}+Bx{e}^{x}+B{e}^{x}-4{e}^{2x}.
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(0)=0$ into the derivative gives

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =A{e}^{0}+B(0){e}^{0}+B{e}^{0}-4{e}^{2(0)} \\ 0 & =A+B-4 \\ 0 & =2+B-4 \\ B & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $A=2$ and $B=2,$ we have the following solution to the initial value problem:

$$
y=2{e}^{x}+2x{e}^{x}-2{e}^{2x}
$$

questions.problem:
Solve the initial value problem

$$
{y}^{″}+6{y}^{′}+10y=-6{e}^{-2x},\,y(\frac{\pi }{2})={e}^{-\pi },\text{ }\text{ }{y}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2})=-2{e}^{-\pi }.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x),$ which is the solution to the homogeneous equation

$$
{y}^{″}+6{y}^{′}+10y=0.
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
{\lambda }^{2}+6\lambda +10=0.
$$

The auxiliary equation can be solved by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+6\lambda +10 & =0 \\ ({\lambda }^{2}+6\lambda +9)-9+10 & =0 \\ (\lambda +3)^{2}+1 & =0 \\ (\lambda +3)^{2} & =-1 \\ \lambda +3 & =\pm \text{i} \\ \lambda  & =-3\pm \text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,  the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{c}(x) & ={e}^{-3x}(P\operatorname{cos}⁡x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡x).\end{aligned}
$$

We now need to find the particular integral ${y}_{p}(x).$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is $-6{e}^{-2x}.$ In this case, the constant factor in the exponent is $-2$, which is not the root of the auxiliary equation. Therefore, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}=\alpha {e}^{-2x},
$$

where $\alpha $ is a constant that is to be determined.

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives:

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=-2\alpha {e}^{-2x},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=4\alpha {e}^{-2x}
$$

We substitute ${y}_{p},$ ${y}_{p}^{′},$ and ${y}_{p}^{″}$ into the ODE and solve for $\alpha :$

$$
\begin{aligned}4\alpha {e}^{-2x}+6(-2\alpha {e}^{-2x})+10(\alpha {e}^{-2x}) & =-6{e}^{-2x} \\ (4-12+10)\alpha {e}^{-2x} & =-6{e}^{-2x} \\ 2\alpha  & =-6 \\ \alpha  & =-3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=-3{e}^{-2x}.
$$

The general solution is given by

$$
y(x)={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x),
$$

and therefore, the general solution in our case is

$$
y={e}^{-3x}(P\operatorname{cos}⁡x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡x)-3{e}^{-2x}.
$$

Now let's find the constants $P$ and $Q.$ 

Substituting $y(\frac{\pi }{2})={e}^{-\pi }$ into the general solution gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}Q{e}^{-3\pi /2}-3{e}^{-\pi } & ={e}^{-\pi } \\ Q{e}^{-3\pi /2} & =4{e}^{-\pi } \\ Q & =4{e}^{\pi /2}\end{aligned}
$$

We now need to apply the condition ${y}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2})=-2{e}^{-\pi }.$ First, we differentiate $y$ to find ${y}^{′}$:

$$
{y}^{′}=(Q-3P){e}^{-3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-(P+3Q){e}^{-3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+6{e}^{-2x}
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2})=-2{e}^{-\pi }$ into the above gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}-(P+3Q){e}^{-3\pi /2}+6{e}^{-\pi } & =-2{e}^{-\pi } \\ -(P+12{e}^{\pi /2}){e}^{-3\pi /2} & =-8{e}^{-\pi } \\ -P{e}^{-3\pi /2}-12{e}^{-\pi } & =-8{e}^{-\pi } \\ -P{e}^{-3\pi /2} & =4{e}^{-\pi } \\ P & =-4{e}^{\pi /2}\end{aligned}
$$

So we have $P=-4{e}^{\pi /2}$ and $Q=4{e}^{\pi /2}.$

We substitute this into the general particular integral and find that the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =(-4{e}^{\pi /2}){e}^{-3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+(4{e}^{\pi /2}){e}^{-3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-3{e}^{-2x} \\ y & =4{e}^{-3x+\pi /2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-3{e}^{-2x}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+5\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+6y=4{e}^{-2x}
$$

has the general solution

$$
y(x)=A{e}^{-3x}+B{e}^{-2x}+4x{e}^{-2x},
$$

solve the initial value problem

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+5\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+6y=4{e}^{-2x},\,y(0)=1,\,{y}^{′}(0)=1.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
We find the constants $A$ and $B$ by substituting the initial conditions.

- Substituting $y(0)=1$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =A{e}^{-3(0)}+B{e}^{-2(0)}+4(0){e}^{-2(0)} \\ 1 & =A+B.\end{aligned}
$$

- Differentiating $y$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=-3A{e}^{-3x}-2B{e}^{-2x}-8x{e}^{-2x}+4{e}^{-2x}.
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(0)=1$ into the derivative gives

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =-3A{e}^{-3(0)}-2B{e}^{-2(0)}-8(0){e}^{-2(0)}+4{e}^{-2(0)} \\ 1 & =-3A-2B+4 \\ -3 & =-3A-2B.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following system of equations for $A$ and $B:$

$$
{\begin{aligned}A+B=1 \\ -3A-2B=-3\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $A=1,B=0.$

Finally, since $A=1$ and $B=0,$ we have the following solution to the initial value problem:

$$
y={e}^{-3x}+4x{e}^{-2x}
$$

questions.problem:
Solve the initial value problem

$$
{y}^{″}-{y}^{′}-12y=10{e}^{2x},\,y(0)=0,\text{ }\text{ }{y}^{′}(0)=2.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x),$ which is the solution to the homogeneous equation

$$
{y}^{″}-{y}^{′}-12y=0.
$$

Writing down and solving the auxiliary equation gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-\lambda -12 & =0 \\ (\lambda +3)(\lambda -4) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So $\lambda =-3$ or $\lambda =4$, and therefore the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{-3x}+B{e}^{4x}.
$$

We now need to find the particular integral ${y}_{p}(x).$
The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is $10{e}^{2x}.$ In this case, the constant factor in the exponent is $2$, which is not the root of the auxiliary equation. Therefore, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}=\alpha {e}^{2x},
$$

where $\alpha $ is a constant that is to be determined.

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=2\alpha {e}^{2x},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=4\alpha {e}^{2x}\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute ${y}_{p},$ ${y}_{p}^{′},$ and ${y}_{p}^{″}$ into the ODE and solve for $\alpha :$

$$
\begin{aligned}4\alpha {e}^{2x}-2\alpha {e}^{2x}-12(\alpha {e}^{2x}) & =10{e}^{2x} \\ \alpha (4-2-12){e}^{2x} & =10{e}^{2x} \\ -10\alpha {e}^{2x} & =10{e}^{2x} \\ -10\alpha  & =10 \\ \alpha  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=-{e}^{2x}.
$$

The general solution is given by

$$
y(x)={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x),
$$

and therefore, the general solution in our case is

$$
y=A{e}^{-3x}+B{e}^{4x}-{e}^{2x}.
$$

Let us find constants $A$ and $B.$ 

Substituting $y(0)=0$ into the general solution gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}A+B-1 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

We now need to apply the condition ${y}^{′}(0)=2.$ First, we differentiate $y$ to find ${y}^{′}$:

$$
{y}^{′}=-3A{e}^{-3x}+4B{e}^{4x}-2{e}^{2x}
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(0)=2$ into the above gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}-3A+4B-2 & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following system of equations for $A$ and $B$:

$$
{\begin{aligned}A+B=1 \\ -3A+4B=4\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $A=0,B=1.$

We substitute this into the general particular integral and find that the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y={e}^{4x}-{e}^{2x}.
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}^2 y}{\textrm{d} x^2} + \frac{\textrm{d} y}{\textrm{d} x} - 2y = 20 e ^ {3x}.
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we find the complementary solution by solving the associated homogeneous ODE. Since the roots of the characteristic equation are $\lambda = 1, -2,$ we get

$$
y_c  = Ae^{x} + Be^{- 2 x}.
$$

Second, we find a particular solution of the inhomogeneous ODE. We see that the right-hand side is $20e^{3x},$ and $e^{3x}$ is not a term in the complementary solution, so we assume that a particular solution takes the form 

$$
y_p = \alpha e^{3x},
$$

where $\alpha$ is a constant to be determined.

Calculating the first and second derivatives of $y_p,$ we get

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}y_p}{\textrm{d}x} = 3 \alpha e ^{3x},
\quad \frac{\textrm{d}^2y_p}{\textrm{d}x^2} = 9  \alpha e ^{3x}.
$$

To find the value of $\alpha,$  we substitute the derivatives into the original ODE and get

$$
\begin{aligned}9\alpha {e}^{3x}+3\alpha {e}^{3x}-2\alpha {e}^{3x} & =20{e}^{3x} \\ \alpha (9+3-2){e}^{3x} & =20{e}^{3x} \\ 10\alpha {e}^{3x} & =20{e}^{3x} \\ 10\alpha  & =20 \\ \alpha  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the particular solution is 

$$
y_p = 2e^{3x}
$$

and the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={y}_{c}+{y}_{p} \\  & =A{e}^{x}+B{e}^{-2x}+2{e}^{3x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Find the general solution to the equation

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}^2 y}{\textrm{d} x^2} - 6\frac{\textrm{d} y}{\textrm{d} x} + 9y = e ^{3x}.
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we find the complementary solution by solving the associated homogeneous ODE. Since the characteristic equation has a single repeated root $\lambda = 3,$ the complementary solution is

$$
y_c(x) = Ae^{3x} + Bxe^{3x}.
$$

Second, we find a particular solution of the inhomogeneous ODE. We see that the right-hand side is $e^{3x},$ and $e^{3x}$ and $xe^{3x}$ are both terms in the complementary solution, so we assume that a particular solution takes the form 

$$
y_p = \alpha x^2e ^ {3x},
$$

where $\alpha$ is a constant to be determined.

Calculating the first and second derivatives of $y_p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x} & =(3{x}^{2}+2x)\alpha {e}^{3x},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=(9{x}^{2}+12x+2)\alpha {e}^{3x}.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute $y_p$, $y'_p$ and $y_p''$ into the ODE and solve for $\alpha\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}(9{x}^{2}+12x+2)\alpha {e}^{3x}-6(3{x}^{2}+2x)\alpha {e}^{3x}+9\alpha {x}^{2}{e}^{3x} & ={e}^{3x} \\ (9{x}^{2}+12x+2-18{x}^{2}-12x+9{x}^{2})\alpha {e}^{3x} & ={e}^{3x} \\ 2\alpha {e}^{3x} & ={e}^{3x} \\ 2\alpha  & =1 \\ \alpha  & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
y_p(x) = \dfrac 1 2x^2 e ^{3x},
$$

and the general solution is 

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={y}_{c}+{y}_{p} \\  & =A{e}^{3x}+Bx{e}^{3x}+\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}{e}^{3x}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Given that the differential equation

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}^2 y}{\textrm{d} x^2} - 6\frac{\textrm{d} y}{\textrm{d} x} + 9y = e ^{3x}
$$

has the general solution

$$
Ae^{3 x} + Bxe^{3 x} + \dfrac 1 2 x ^2 e^{3 x},
$$

solve the initial value problem

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}^2 y}{\textrm{d} x^2} - 6\frac{\textrm{d} y}{\textrm{d} x} + 9y = e ^{3x}, \qquad y(0) = 2 , \ \ y'(0) = 1.
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We find the constants $A$ and $B$ by substituting the initial conditions.

- Substituting $y(0)=2$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =A{e}^{0}+B(0){e}^{0}+\frac{1}{2}(0)^{2}{e}^{0} \\ 2 & =A.\end{aligned}
$$

- Differentiating $y$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}=3A{e}^{3x}+B{e}^{3x}+3Bx{e}^{3x}+x{e}^{3x}+\frac{3}{2}{x}^{2}{e}^{3x},\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $y'(0)=1$ into the derivative gives

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =3A{e}^{0}+B{e}^{0}+3B(0){e}^{0}+0{e}^{0}+\frac{3}{2}(0)^{2}{e}^{0} \\ 1 & =3A+B \\ 1 & =3(2)+B \\ -5 & =B.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $A=2$ and $B=-5,$ we have the following solution to the initial value problem:

$$
\begin{aligned}y=2{e}^{3x}-5x{e}^{3x}+\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}{e}^{3x}\end{aligned}
$$
